Summary

This paper studies hybrid reinforcement learning in linear MDPs, where an agent has both an offline dataset and the ability to collect online data. The paper considers two hybrid paradigms: (i) online-to-offline, where reward-agnostic online exploration augments offline data before offline policy learning, and (ii) offline-to-online, where an online regret minimization algorithm is warm-started using offline data. The main contributions are two algorithms: RAPPEL for PAC learning and HYRULE for regret minimization. The claimed results improve over prior hybrid RL guarantees for linear MDPs, avoid single-policy concentrability assumptions, and in some regimes improve over the best offline-only or online-only rates.

Overall assessment

The paper addresses an important and timely question in hybrid RL: whether one can provably beat the barriers of purely offline or purely online learning in non-tabular settings without relying on strong concentrability assumptions. The focus on linear MDPs is well motivated, and the paper’s high-level message is interesting: hybrid RL can indeed yield sharper guarantees than either source alone, even under weak assumptions on the behavior policy.

The paper is ambitious and technically substantial. The split between online-to-offline and offline-to-online approaches is conceptually useful, and the comparison to prior work is generally clear. The claimed improvements in horizon dependence and partition-adaptive dimension dependence are potentially significant. If all results are correct, this would be a meaningful contribution to the theory of hybrid RL.

That said, I have several concerns about clarity, assumptions, presentation, and the practical/theoretical interpretation of the guarantees. My main reservations are not about the importance of the problem, but about whether the paper currently presents the results in a sufficiently precise and convincing way for a top conference. In particular, some assumptions seem stronger or less innocuous than the paper suggests, some theorem statements are hard to parse, and the empirical section is too limited relative to the scope of the claims.

Strengths

1. Important problem setting
The paper tackles a central open question in hybrid RL theory beyond the tabular case. Extending “hybrid beats offline-only/online-only” phenomena to linear MDPs is a natural and valuable direction.

2. Two complementary hybrid paradigms
It is a strength that the paper studies both PAC-style online-to-offline learning and regret-minimizing offline-to-online learning. This gives a broader perspective than papers focusing on only one hybrid mode.

3. Potentially strong theoretical improvements
The claimed bounds improve over prior hybrid RL results in linear MDPs, especially in horizon dependence. The partition-based dependence on c_off(X_off) and d_on is also appealing and aligns with the intuition that offline data may cover only part of the relevant feature space.

4. Computational efficiency
The algorithms are based on known computationally efficient primitives (OPTCOV, LinPEVI-ADV+, LSVI-UCB++), which makes the results more compelling than purely information-theoretic statements.

5. Good positioning relative to prior work
The introduction and tables do a reasonable job of situating the paper relative to prior hybrid RL literature.

Weaknesses and concerns

1. The assumptions around the partition and coverability need much more scrutiny

A central theme of the paper is that the guarantees hold “without single-policy concentrability.” While this is true in a literal sense, the replacement assumptions deserve more careful discussion.

For RAPPEL, Assumption 2 requires c_on(X_on) < infinity for any partition, equivalently a full-rank projected covariate condition. This is not a benign assumption. In fact, it appears to encode a fairly strong explorability requirement over the online partition. The paper argues this can be achieved “for any linear MDP by transforming the features to project them onto the eigenspace corresponding to the nonzero singular values,” but this explanation is not fully convincing. Projecting onto the nonzero eigenspace of the offline covariance does not by itself guarantee that the online-reachable feature subspace is fully explorable at every stage h in the sense required by Assumption 2. More importantly, changing the feature representation after seeing offline data may alter the interpretation of d_on and c_off in a way that makes the guarantee less intrinsic than advertised.

Relatedly, Lemma 1 states that for any partition, c_on(X_on) <= d_on. This is a strong and somewhat surprising statement. Since c_on is defined via an inf over policies and a smallest nonzero eigenvalue of an occupancy-induced covariance, I would expect this to depend on the geometry/reachability structure of the MDP, not only on subspace dimension. If this lemma is correct, it is quite important and deserves much more intuition and discussion in the main text. As written, it feels under-explained.

For HYRULE, the theorem takes an infimum over all partitions, which is elegant, but it also raises interpretational questions. Since c_off(X_off) depends on the partition and the offline occupancy covariance projected onto that partition, the result may be difficult to instantiate or compare in concrete settings. The paper should provide at least one nontrivial example showing how the optimal partition behaves and when the bound is substantially better than d-based rates.

2. The theorem statements are difficult to parse and sometimes feel over-claimed

Theorem 1 is especially hard to interpret. It gives two different upper bounds inside a min, with additional conditions involving alpha_off, alpha_on, N*(tau), and a tolerance choice tau <= \tilde O(max{...}). It is not clear what the recommended parameter setting is, what regime each term is intended for, and which bound should be viewed as the main result. The prose later emphasizes an H^3-style sample complexity, but the theorem statement itself still contains H^4 terms in one branch and a more complicated second branch with squared c_off and d_on factors. The practical and conceptual takeaway is therefore muddled.

Similarly, Theorem 2 requires N_on, N_off = \tilde \Omega(d^13 H^14), which is extremely large. Even if this is only a burn-in artifact of the proof, it substantially weakens the practical significance of the result. The paper acknowledges nontrivial burn-in costs, but the theorem should be discussed more candidly. A result that improves asymptotic regret while requiring such enormous polynomial thresholds is theoretically interesting, but the presentation currently overemphasizes “breaking barriers” without equally emphasizing the cost.

3. The comparison to lower bounds is somewhat slippery

The title and abstract suggest that hybrid RL “breaks sample size barriers” in linear MDPs. But the actual results do not appear to establish a new minimax lower bound for hybrid RL, nor do they show a uniform improvement over both offline-only and online-only minimax rates simultaneously. Rather, they show that in certain decomposed forms, the hybrid bounds are no worse than one baseline and can improve depending on the partition and data quality.

This is still interesting, but the framing should be more precise. For example:
- RAPPEL is compared mainly to offline-only error bounds and prior hybrid PAC bounds.
- HYRULE is compared mainly to online-only regret bounds and prior hybrid regret bounds.
- The paper itself notes in the discussion that it still lacks an algorithm that simultaneously improves both the best offline-only and online-only rates at once.

Given that caveat, the title feels somewhat too strong. The paper does not fully “break sample size barriers” in a universal sense; it gives improved guarantees under a partition-based decomposition and separate objectives.

4. The empirical section is too weak for the scope of the claims

The experiments are limited and mostly illustrative. They do not validate the main theoretical phenomena in a convincing way.

Specific issues:
- Only one environment is used, a scaled-down Tetris benchmark.
- The implementation deviates from the theory: Algorithm 2 uses LSVI-UCB++ “as-is,” and Algorithm 1 substitutes LSVI-UCB for FORCE within OPTCOV and LinPEVI-ADV for LinPEVI-ADV+. These substitutions may be reasonable for engineering purposes, but they weaken the connection between experiments and theory.
- There is no systematic study of how performance varies with offline data quality, N_off, N_on, horizon, or feature dimension.
- There is no empirical examination of the partition quantities c_off(X_off) or d_on, despite these being central to the theory.
- The regret plot uses only 10 trials and appears fairly small-scale.

As a result, the experiments support the intuition that offline warm-starting can help and that reward-agnostic exploration can complement poor offline data, but they do not strongly validate the paper’s specific theoretical claims.

5. Clarity and exposition need improvement

The paper is often difficult to read. There are many grammatical issues, awkward phrasings, and theorem statements that are hard to follow. Some examples:
- Frequent passive constructions and unusual wording (“it is achieved by RAPPEL,” “we observe that,” “we propose that c_on < infinity”) make the text less precise.
- Several definitions and assumptions are introduced in a way that obscures their meaning.
- The notation is heavy and sometimes inconsistent.
- The proof sketches are dense and not very intuitive.

This matters because the paper’s contribution is largely theoretical. For such a paper, precision and readability are essential.

6. Some technical claims deserve more justification in the main text

A few examples:
- The claimed typo in He et al. (2023) may be correct, but if the paper relies on modifying a variance floor from H to sqrt(H), this should be handled carefully. It is risky to build part of the algorithm statement around an asserted typo in prior work without a more formal justification.
- The statement that there always exists a partition such that c_off(X_off) = O(d) is important, but not enough by itself to explain when the partition-adaptive bound is substantially better than the baseline.
- The truncation argument appears central to the H^3 dependence, but the main text explanation is too compressed to assess whether the argument is robust or whether hidden constants/polylogs are severe.

Questions for the authors

1. Can you provide a clearer interpretation of Assumption 2? In what sense is it weaker than standard explorability assumptions used in reward-free or reward-agnostic exploration for linear MDPs? Can you give an example where single-policy concentrability fails badly but Assumption 2 still holds naturally?

2. Lemma 1 claims c_on(X_on) <= d_on for any partition. Can you provide more intuition in the main text for why this is true? This seems surprisingly strong.

3. For Theorem 1, what is the cleanest corollary one should remember? Is the intended takeaway
   sqrt(c_off d H^3 min{c_off,H}/N_off) + sqrt(d_on d H^3 min{d_on,H}/N_on)?
If so, can the theorem be reorganized around that expression more directly?

4. For Theorem 2, how essential is the very large burn-in condition N_on, N_off = \tilde \Omega(d^13 H^14)? Is this inherited from LSVI-UCB++ analysis, from the partition decomposition, or from the truncation argument? Could a weaker but cleaner theorem be stated?

5. Since HYRULE takes an infimum over partitions but does not know the partition, can you explain more concretely how the proof identifies the partition-adaptive decomposition? Is this purely an analysis device, or does the algorithm implicitly exploit geometry in a way that could be diagnosed empirically?

6. Can you provide experiments varying N_off and N_on, and perhaps comparing against Tan and Xu (2024) or a closer hybrid baseline? The current experiments do not really test the claimed scaling improvements.

Suggestions for improvement

1. Clarify the main theorem statements
I strongly recommend rewriting Theorems 1 and 2 to separate:
- the exact formal statement,
- the clean corollary,
- the regime where improvement occurs,
- the baseline recovered in the worst case.

2. Better discuss assumptions
The paper should be more transparent about what replaces single-policy concentrability. In particular, Assumption 2 should be discussed as a substantive explorability assumption, not merely a technicality.

3. Strengthen the empirical section
At minimum:
- vary offline data quality and quantity,
- vary online budget,
- compare to stronger baselines,
- report sensitivity to feature dimension/projection rank,
- explain how the practical partition intuition manifests.

4. Improve exposition and proofreading
The paper would benefit from substantial editing for grammar, notation, and readability.

5. Moderate the framing
The title and abstract should better reflect that the paper gives improved guarantees in linear MDPs under partition-based decompositions, rather than universally surpassing both offline-only and online-only lower bounds in all senses.

Recommendation

Weak reject / borderline

Rationale

I think the problem is important and the claimed results are potentially significant. There is real novelty here, especially in extending hybrid improvements to linear MDPs and in handling both PAC and regret settings. However, in its current form, the paper does not yet make the contribution as convincingly as it should. The assumptions and theorem statements need clearer interpretation, the empirical support is limited, and the presentation is difficult to follow. If the technical results are correct, this could become a strong paper after revision, but I am not fully convinced by the current version.

Confidence

Medium. I am reasonably confident in my assessment of significance, clarity, and empirical weakness. My confidence on the deepest technical details is moderate rather than high because many proofs are deferred and the presentation makes them hard to verify from the main text alone.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper studies hybrid reinforcement learning in linear MDPs, where an agent has both an offline dataset and the ability to collect online data. It proposes two computationally efficient algorithms: RAPPEL, an online-to-offline method that performs reward-agnostic exploration to augment offline data before running pessimistic offline RL, and HYRULE, an offline-to-online method that warm-starts an optimistic online RL algorithm using offline data. The main claims are that these methods avoid single-policy concentrability assumptions, improve over prior hybrid RL guarantees for linear MDPs, and can achieve bounds that are no worse than the best known offline-only or online-only guarantees, with potential improvements depending on the quality and quantity of offline/online data. The paper also provides experiments in a scaled-down Tetris environment suggesting empirical benefits of both approaches.
strengths: Addresses an important open question in hybrid RL with function approximation, extending beyond the tabular setting to linear MDPs.
Provides two complementary algorithmic frameworks, one for PAC learning and one for regret minimization, which makes the contribution broader and more practically relevant.
Theoretical guarantees appear stronger than prior hybrid RL results in linear MDPs, especially in horizon dependence and partition-dependent dimension terms.
Avoids relying on single-policy concentrability, which is a meaningful conceptual advance over much prior work.
Builds on established algorithmic primitives (OPTCOV, pessimistic offline RL, LSVI-UCB++) in a principled way, making the methods computationally plausible.
The partition-based analysis separating offline-covered and online-needed subspaces is intuitive and potentially useful beyond this paper.
Includes experiments that qualitatively support the claimed benefits of hybridization under poor offline coverage.
weaknesses: The presentation is often hard to follow, with many claims stated informally and heavy dependence on appendices for key arguments.
Several assumptions and quantities are nonstandard or operationally unclear, especially the partition choice, the tolerance selection for RAPPEL, and how these would be instantiated in practice.
The burn-in/sample size requirements are extremely large (e.g., Theorem 2 requires quantities on the order of d^13 H^14), which weakens the practical significance of the regret result.

The claimed improvements are sometimes qualified in ways that make the practical gain less clear; for example, some bounds still contain squared partial concentrability terms or large hidden polynomial factors.
The experimental section is relatively limited and does not rigorously validate the theory; implementations also substitute different algorithms for the theoretically analyzed components.
The comparison to prior work is mostly asymptotic and may understate tradeoffs introduced by stronger assumptions such as projected full-rank explorability for Algorithm 1.
Some notation and statements appear inconsistent or awkwardly phrased, making it difficult to verify whether all theorem statements are fully precise from the main text alone.
soundness_issues: Algorithm 1 relies on Assumption 2 (full-rank projected covariates / bounded partial coverability), which is substantial and may be close in spirit to requiring strong explorability of the online partition; the paper argues it can be enforced by feature projection, but this changes the representation and may not preserve the intended problem class without further justification.

Theorem 1 requires choosing the OPTCOV tolerance using quantities such as d_on and c_off(X_off), but these depend on an unknown partition and coverage properties; this weakens the algorithmic realizability of the guarantee.

Theorem 2's guarantee is adaptive to the best partition in analysis, but the proof sketch suggests nontrivial decomposition arguments and large lower bounds on N_on and N_off; without checking appendices, it is hard to fully assess whether all steps are tight and whether hidden constants/polylogs are manageable.

The experiments do not faithfully implement all theoretically analyzed algorithms (e.g., substitutions for FORCE and LinPEVI-ADV+), so they provide only indirect evidence for the exact theoretical claims.

The claim that hybrid RL 'breaks sample size barriers' is directionally supported by the bounds, but the improvements are instance/partition dependent rather than uniformly better in all regimes, so the title may overstate the universality of the result.
